opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing I'm most optimistic about in the near term is the stuff that's a little less flashy than the demos you see on Twitter. I think the clearest early wins are going to be in domains where the work is long-horizon enough that a single prompt-and-response doesn't cut it, but where you can still verify whether the agent did a good job. Coding is the obvious example. We've already seen agents go from autocompleting a line to taking a task, exploring a codebase, running tests, and iterating until something works. That loop of act, observe, correct is where agents really shine, and code gives you that feedback signal almost for free.

The second area I'm excited about is research and analysis: things like digging through a bunch of sources, synthesizing them, and coming back with something useful. A lot of knowledge work is basically "go find out what's true about X and summarize it in a way I can act on." Agents are getting genuinely good at that, and even when they're not perfect, they compress hours of work into minutes, and the human can review the output.

What ties those together, and what I'd encourage people building with these tools to think about, is matching the task to the reliability. Agents today aren't flawless, so the near-term sweet spot is tasks where the cost of a mistake is low or the mistake is easy to catch, and the value of saving time is high. If you pick problems with that shape, you can get a ton of value right now, and as the models improve, the frontier of what's safe to hand off keeps expanding. That's what makes me optimistic. It's not some distant future thing. People are getting real leverage out of this today.

r001.rationale: The response describes agentic tools saving time on coding and research, but does not say they can get valuable work done that would otherwise remain undone because people lack time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the thing I'm most optimistic about in the near term is kind of boring, which is why I like it: it's the long tail of work that nobody wants to do and nobody has had the budget to automate.

If you look inside most companies, there's this huge surface area of tasks that are too small or too idiosyncratic to justify building a dedicated piece of software for. Reconciling two spreadsheets that don't quite match. Pulling data out of PDFs that come in slightly different formats from every vendor. Chasing down the status of something across three internal tools and writing a summary. Historically, the only way to handle that was to throw people at it, and the people doing it were usually overqualified and bored. What's changed is that an agent can now look at a task like that, figure out roughly what to do, use the tools you'd use, and get it mostly right. And when it gets it wrong, the cost of a human checking the output is way lower than the cost of a human doing the whole thing.

So I'm less excited about the "agent replaces a knowledge worker" framing and more excited about agents eating the plumbing. That's where the near-term value is, because it doesn't require the models to be perfect. It requires them to be good enough that supervision is cheaper than execution, and in a lot of domains we're already there.

The second thing, which is closer to my own work, is software engineering specifically. Coding is the domain where agents are furthest along, partly because feedback is so concrete. You can run the tests. You can compile the thing. The agent can check its own work in a way it can't for, say, writing a strategy memo. And what I see happening is that the unit of work engineers hand off is getting bigger. A year or two ago it was autocomplete. Then it was "write this function." Now people are reasonably comfortable saying "go fix this bug, here's the issue," walking away, and coming back to a pull request. I think that keeps expanding, and the interesting question becomes less "can the model code" and more "how do you build the harness, the evals, the guardrails, so that you trust it with bigger chunks."

The caveat I'd put on all of this is that the optimism is about the next couple of years, not next quarter. The demos are way ahead of the deployed reality. Getting an agent to work reliably in production is still a lot of unglamorous engineering: defining what success looks like, building evaluation, figuring out where the human should be in the loop. But that's a tractable problem, and it's the kind of problem the industry is good at grinding through. So I'm optimistic, just with a healthy respect for how much work is between here and there.

r001.rationale: The response presents automating small, idiosyncratic tasks as a near-term opportunity, but attributes the lack of automation to insufficient budget and says people handled the work. It does not clearly identify valuable work left undone because human time is limited.

astra-6.text:
I’m most optimistic about coding. There’s a tight feedback loop: an agent can make a change, run the tests, see what failed, and try again. That gives it a way to check whether it’s making progress, which is harder in a lot of other domains.

And I think the opportunity is broader than writing new code. A lot of engineering work is figuring out how a system works, tracking down a bug, or making a change across a bunch of files. Having an agent take a first pass at that, with a human reviewing the result, can be really valuable.

So in the near term, I’m excited about tasks where you can give the agent a clear objective and a way to verify its work. You don’t need to hand over an entire job to get a lot of benefit.

r001.rationale: The response describes useful engineering work agents can assist with, but does not say this work would otherwise remain undone because human time is limited.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m most optimistic about tasks where there’s a clear way to check whether the agent did a good job. Coding is a great example: you can make a change, run tests, look at the errors, and iterate. That feedback loop gives the agent a way to make progress without a person having to supervise every step.

I think there’s a lot of opportunity in extending that pattern to other kinds of work. You give the agent a well-scoped task, the tools it needs, and some way to evaluate the result. It does the legwork, and a human reviews the outcome. That’s useful even before you get to agents that can reliably handle an entire job on their own.

r001.rationale: The response highlights tasks agents can do with limited supervision and says they can handle the legwork, but it does not identify work that would otherwise remain undone because people lack time.
